keyVerseText: The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מִלָּה (millâh) derives from the root מָלַל (mâlal), which means to speak or utter. This root emphasizes the act of verbal expression, highlighting the transition from the internal intention to external speech. Thus, מִלָּה carries the fundamental sense of a spoken word or utterance, going beyond a mere written or abstract concept to focus on the living, vocalized communication.
usageInScripture: Throughout Scripture, מִלָּה appears 38 times, predominantly in poetic contexts such as the book of Job, where it conveys 'word,' 'speech,' or 'utterance.' The term is consistently translated as 'words' in various forms, reflecting both singular and collective expressions of speech. This range indicates that מִלָּה encompasses everything from a single spoken word to an extended discourse or thematic topic, underscoring its versatility in describing divine and human communication.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִלָּה as a spoken word or utterance enriches our grasp of how God reveals Himself and interacts with humanity. The word emphasizes that divine revelation is not static but communicated dynamically through speech, embodying God’s personal engagement with His people. This aligns with the Christian faith’s affirmation of the Word made flesh in Jesus Christ, who is the ultimate expression of God's living speech. Recognizing מִלָּה as both individual words and collective discourse invites believers to cherish Scripture as the living voice of God, calling for attentive listening and faithful response.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 23:2, 'The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue,' the term מִלָּה highlights the divine origin and authoritative nature of the speech delivered. The word here signifies not just any utterance but the Spirit-inspired message that carries God's power and truth. This underscores that the prophet’s words are not merely human thoughts but the very speech of God, making the verse a profound testament to the divine inspiration behind Scripture.
